claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is an as-solidified, homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
The dynamic strength–ductility balance of Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by a shift in dislocation mechanisms.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi reduces the stacking-fault energy.
Stacking-fault energy modulates the relative ease of dislocation cross-slip and twinning.
The composition-induced reduction in stacking-fault energy makes cross-slip easier.
The composition-induced reduction in stacking-fault energy may enhance deformation twinning at particular temperatures and strain rates.
Low temperatures and high strain rates increase activation of cross-slip and/or twinning in the Co-free alloy.
Increased cross-slip and/or twinning enhances strain-rate sensitivity and changes strength–ductility performance.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will show a more pronounced increase in flow stress at low temperatures and/or high strain rates.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn may show a shifted balance between work hardening and ductility at low temperatures and/or high strain rates.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit a lower activation volume than the Co-containing baseline.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit more twins or cross-slip features than the Co-containing baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies where dislocation behavior is sensitive to stacking-fault-energy changes.
At very high temperatures where diffusion dominates, the proposed stacking-fault-energy-mediated mechanism may cease to be the primary factor.
Short-range ordering or other atomic-scale effects may also contribute to the temperature- and strain-rate-dependent behavior.
A controlled comparison should test Co-free FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi at matched temperatures and strain rates.
The hypothesis is falsified if the alloys show no significant differences in strain-rate sensitivity, activation volume, or dislocation substructure under the specified conditions.
